title: What if You Could Turn The Annual Performance Review Ritual Into a Development Opportunity?
author: Kurt Mueller
source: Rookie to Pro: The Hidden Side of Leadership (kurtmueller.substack.com), November 7, 2026
summary: Kurt Mueller proposes that the annual performance review should look backward only long enough to establish where an employee has been and then spend most of its time on where they are going. He argues that most real performance management has already happened before the review, through weekly or biweekly collaborative one-to-ones that surface accomplishments, obstacles and problems while there is still time to act. Those conversations also build a shared record of the whole period, which counters recency bias and invites employees to contribute their own evidence. The forward-looking half asks about upcoming challenges, new responsibilities, capabilities to build and career direction, with the aim of leaving with a development commitment rather than a completed form. Mueller acknowledges that ratings and pay recommendations are still required and urges leaders to be honest about what they can and cannot influence. He closes with a simple first step: one collaborative conversation with each employee before the next review.
points: A no-surprises review depends on regular one-to-ones that address performance problems promptly instead of saving feedback for December.
Co-creating a running record of the performance period reduces recency bias and makes the review more transparent and evidence-based.
Most of the review conversation should look forward, covering challenges, new responsibilities, capabilities and career direction.
The goal is a development commitment, not simply a completed evaluation form.
Leaders should be candid about what they can influence in ratings and pay, and avoid promising rewards they cannot deliver.
quotes: Here’s my proposition: The most productive annual performance review looks backward just long enough to establish where you’ve been, then focuses on where you’re going.

Start conducting weekly or biweekly collaborative 1:1 conversations. These aren’t simply status updates. They’re opportunities to discuss accomplishments, assess progress against expectations, identify obstacles, and address performance problems while there’s still time to correct them.
The annual review should confirm what employees already know, not introduce unwelcome surprises.
Without that record, it’s easy to fall into recency bias , placing too much weight on what happened during the last few weeks rather than evaluating the full performance period.
Invite employees to contribute their own evidence of accomplishments, challenges overcome, skills developed, and improvements made and continuing needs.
The objective is to leave with a development commitment, not simply a completed evaluation form.
When that’s the case, explain honestly what you can and cannot influence. Don’t promise rewards you cannot deliver.
You may not control your organization’s performance review system. But you can transform what your employees experience.
